newsitem.title: INDIA: India has to do lot more to attract oil majors - BZW.
newsitem.headline: India has to do lot more to attract oil majors - BZW.

text.p: India will have to make itself more attractive before global oil majors invest in the country, a senior official of Barclays Group said on Tuesday.
"The budget has made an excellent start in liberalising fiscal terms," Richard Oliver, co-head of BZW, the investment banking arm of U.K.'s Barclays Group told a seminar.
"But a lot remains to be done," he said.
Oliver said India did not appear to be a priority for oil majors. Only one out of the top 25 oil majors -- Royal Dutch/Shell -- had a presence in India, he said.
Oliver said BZW asked the oil majors why they were not keen on India and received a variety of answers.
One oil major said geological data suggested that there were not many more oil reserves left beyond what had already been discovered.

Another oil major told BZW the Indian bureaucracy made operating in India difficult. Other reasons were a lack of sufficiently attractive economic terms and lack of knowledge among potential Indian partners.
Oliver said he did not agree with the last observation -- on poor knowledge of Indian firms -- and BZW's own experience in the field proved the contrary.
But the other concerns needed to be addressed, he said.
He said the competition for international capital was not only among nations but between industries such as oil and power.
Analysts said India's energy consumption was growing at over 8.0 percent a year and a third of its foreign exchange was spent on import of petroleum products.
More than half of India's annual consumption of about 70 million tonnes of petroleum products is met through imports.

India announced a new exploration policy in its 1997/98 (April-March) budget released last month. It promised local producers Oil and Natural Gas Corp and Oil India international price for oil for new discoveries and freedom for marketing oil and gas in the local market.
To encourage deep water exploration, the government has halved the royalty rates for the first seven years after start of commercial production.
"Every $1.0 per barrel rise in the crude price adds another $400 million peryear to (India's) import bill," securities firm Kleinwort Benson said in its latest research report.
"Every 10 percent rise in demand is equivalent to a 150,000 barrels/day increase in crude oil imports and an additional $1.1 billion on the annual import bill," the report said.
India's petroleum minister T.R. Baalu said on Monday India's per capita consumption of petroleum products is merely 90 kg compared to the world average of 900 kg.
"This alone provides a vast scope for growth and investment in this sector," he said.
